title: Working-parent arrangements trade financial benefit against family and career experience
source_unit: Pew Research Center survey of 2,242 U.S. working parents, March 2-15, 2026, plus Census CPS analysis

observations.period: 2025 CPS analysis; different-sex couples with children under 18

denominator.unit: U.S. different-sex couples with children under 18; arrangement shares

observations.method: Pew Research Center analysis of U.S. Census Bureau Current Population Survey data.
observations.uncertainty: This describes family work arrangements, not hours, income adequacy, care quality, job quality, or household welfare; the comparison is limited to different-sex couples with children under 18.
observations.subgroup: Different-sex couples with children under 18; arrangement patterns also reported by race/ethnicity and education.
observations.counterinterpretation: Two full-time jobs can reflect opportunity, necessity, preference, childcare availability, or cost pressure; a non-employed mother can reflect care choice, health, job access, or household resources.

both_full_time_positive_finances.unit: percent reporting a positive financial impact

dad_full_time_mom_not_employed_positive_.unit: percent of surveyed employed parents in this arrangement reporting a positive child-wellbeing impact; reflects dads' views

both_full_time_positive_children.unit: percent reporting a positive child-wellbeing impact

both_full_time_negative_children.unit: percent reporting a negative child-wellbeing impact

dad_full_time_mom_not_employed_positive_.unit: percent reporting a positive financial impact; reflects dads' views

dad_full_time_mom_not_employed_negative_.unit: percent reporting a negative financial impact; reflects dads' views

observations.method: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey of working parents; family-arrangement groups and perceived impacts are retained as separate descriptive measures.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-sectional self-reports do not identify causality. The sample lacks enough working parents in some gender arrangements for separate analysis, and the non-employed-mother child-wellbeing result reflects employed parents' views, especially fathers in the described group.
observations.subgroup: Working parents by partnered family work arrangement; race, education, and partnership composition differ across groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Parents may evaluate the same arrangement differently depending on income, care access, job flexibility, gender expectations, and prior preferences; positive finances do not prove lower time or care strain.

related_sources.claim: Pew reports work arrangement trends, parent perceptions, childcare challenges, flexibility, and division of family responsibilities.

boundary: This record adds a work-family arrangement and meaning layer. It does not establish that a particular arrangement caused financial security, child outcomes, career effects, gender inequality, or care adequacy, and it does not follow one family through a dated care episode or later recovery.
